name: Mingang Doso
confidence_why: one confirmed first-hand source; 3 other works read were silent
catalog_citation: Benson, Peace & Alexander Andrason. 2022. A Living Grammar Sketch of Mingang Doso, Version 1.1. Salem, OR: Living Tongues Institute for Endangered Languages. 30 pp. CC BY 4.0.
catalog_locator: §2.3 Tone, printed p. 7 = PDF p. 9 of 30 (file the copy we hold)
catalog_quote: Like most Adamawa languages, Mingang Doso is a tonal language and exhibits complex tonal structures. The following tones can be distinguished: high tone [ ́], mid tone [ ̄], and low tone [ ̀], as well as mid falling [ ̂] and, especially in rhetorical questions, low rising [ ᷅]. The tonal patterns are associated with each lexeme and thus the tone is a lexical property of a word. Specific tonal patterns are also exploited to mark questions or communicate certain emotive nuances, e.g., surprise.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The only phonological description states that Mingang Doso is a tonal language with lexically specified tone (H, M, L, mid-falling, low-rising); it makes no statement at all about word stress or accent, so no stress position can be assigned from the literature.
new_statements.exceptions: None on stress; on tone, question/emotive intonation overlays are noted. Norton & Othaniel 2020 (p. 43) add that H and L tones are switched in Doso relative to other Jen varieties (except H after voiced obstruents).
new_statements.domain_note: Tone is stated to be a property of the lexeme (word level); question/emotive tonal patterns operate at the utterance level. The sketch's 'Phonetics' section (consonants, vowels, tone) is under 3 pages, and stress is simply absent from it; it does not explicitly deny word stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Benson & Andrason 2022 describe the speech of Munga village (Bunkaubu, Bugbamui, Mundang quarters), Karim-Lamido LGA, Taraba State — i.e. Mingang Doso proper (ming1254 / mko). Norton & Othaniel 2020 label the same variety 'Doso'; Kleinewillinghöfer 2015 labels it 'MIN = Munga [Məngaŋ] Doso'. Not to be confused with Munga Leelau (LE in Kleinewillinghöfer), a different Bikwin language also called Munga.

The following tones can be distinguished: high tone [ ́ ], mid tone [ ̄ ], and low tone [ ̀ ], as well as mid falling [ ̂ ] and, especially in rhetorical questions, low rising [ ᷅ ]. sources.note: Section 2 'Phonetics' has 2.1 Consonants, 2.2 Vowels, 2.3 Tone (p. 7). States the language is tonal (H, M, L, mid-falling, low-rising) and that tone is a lexical property of each word; questions/emotive nuances use tonal patterns. The words stress/accent/prosody do not occur anywhere in the sketch; no statement on word stress.

sources.note: Comparative phonology of ten Jen varieties incl. Doso (= Mingang Doso, Othaniel's 300-item wordlist). Section 3.3 Tone (pp. 43-45): 'High, mid, low, falling and rising tones were noted.. High and low tones are switched in Doso, except that H does not become L after a voiced obstruent.' Abstract lists nasalisation, tone and breathiness as the prosodic features. No mention of stress or accent anywhere (a full-text search for stress/accent found nothing).
